introduction.text: Largo di Torre Argentina is a historic square in Rome that contains four Roman Republican temples, the remains of Pompey's Theatre, and the site of Julius Caesar's assassination. Its archaeological layers and cultural heritage make it a key window into ancient Roman life and later artistic developments.

history.description: Temple C, the oldest of the four, was built in the 290s/280s BC and probably dedicated to Feronia.
Temple A was constructed in the 3rd century BC, likely as the Temple of Juturna by Gaius Lutatius Catulus.
Temple D dates to the 2nd century BC and was dedicated to the Lares Permarini.
Temple B, a circular tholos, was built in 101 BC by Quintus Lutatius Catulus.
Julius Caesar was assassinated in the Curia of Pompey in 44 BC, a site within the square.
The Teatro Argentina opera house, established in the 18th century, hosted premieres such as Rossini's The Barber of Seville.
After Italian unification, part of Rome was reconstructed in 1909, demolishing the zone of Torre Argentina.
In 1927, a colossal head and arms of a marble statue were discovered during demolition work.
The Torre Argentina Cat Sanctuary was founded in 1993 within Temple D.
In 2019, mayor Virginia Raggi announced walkways to allow public access to the ruins.

design.description: The square contains four Roman Republican temples, each with distinct architectural styles: a rectangular temple, a circular tholos, and a large temple dedicated to sailors.
Largo di Torre Argentina lies within the ancient Campus Martius, surrounded by the Baths of Agrippa, Circus Flaminius, and the Theatre of Pompey.
The Torre Argentina Cat Sanctuary occupies the interior of Temple D, integrating modern facilities with the archaeological site.

art.description: A marble acrolithic statue of Fortuna Huiusce Diei, found during excavations, is now housed in the Centrale Montemartini.
The inner cella of Temple C features a white and black mosaic dating from the restoration after the fire of AD 80.
The apses and frescoes of the early 900s church San Nicola de Calcarario, built on Temple A, remain visible.
